item.title: AI by Default
item.description:
Epistemic status: a good-faith guess at how the world might turn out, after ~30 hours of effort.

This post is an exercise in describing what I think will happen with AI progress "by default", i.e. by attempting to extrapolate various trends and considering their implications, before the next US presidential administration. As a TL;DR, I expect the following:

  • We get many more warning shots.
  • AI is a top-five issue in the election.
  • The best models are withheld for internal use only, on safety grounds.
  • AI-related job displacement is significant enough to show up in the data.
  • Coding and ML R&D are fully automated or require only minimal human oversight.

This is intended to be one representative story of how things might go, in the vein of What 2026 Looks Like and the work of the AI Futures Project. Incidentally, the current AI Futures Model predicts the median date that we get ASI as December 2028 — one month after the election.

The rationale for doing so is largely the same as in What 2026 Looks Like. My goal is to tell a plausible story about what the state of the world might be when we are likely on the brink of RSI, while being suitably deferential to the Gods of Straight Lines. It is intended to be representative of my best-guess modal scenario, given various assumptions:

  • Capabilities keep increasing at the same rate, measured by e.g. METR time horizon, AISI cyber horizon, ECI etc.
  • Safety techniques keep improving at their current rate, with no major breakthroughs.
  • Data centre buildout continues as planned.
  • OpenAI & Anthropic’s capex, revenue etc. continue growing at approximately their current rate.
  • Appetite for aggressive regulation in the US continues to be low.
  • China exhausts less radical policy options before pursuing more radical ones.

Put another way, I am asking what might happen if the shape of these graphs doesn’t change[1]:

I wrote the scenario one quarter at a time, attempting to ensure that the events of each quarter proceed naturally from those of the previous one, rather than making any predictions about 2028 and backchaining. I found this to be a very useful exercise for highlighting parts of my internal model that are low-fidelity (~anything to do with China), and identifying key factors to try to influence (embedded evaluators getting full access to all labs ASAP, avoiding scenarios in which labs themselves become black boxes with internal-only models). I would welcome comments if anything below seems obviously wrong/particularly unlikely.

Q4 2026

Democrats win both chambers on November 3rd, although AI isn’t a defining issue in campaigns despite growing feelings of NIMBYism towards data centres. No new, meaningful federal legislation related to frontier AI is passed. Despite EO 14434, OpenAI does not follow SpaceXSI’s lead and continues to be called OpenAI. Following their signing of the “morally binding” White House Accord, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, SpaceXSI and Nvidia all voluntarily commit to independent third-party evaluators, although on varying terms. Each company gets to choose its own partners, and the partners have differing levels of access within the companies as well as different obligations to the companies with regards to what they publish. Anthropic is the only lab with an evaluator whose publications it can’t veto.

Anthropic’s November IPO is the biggest in history, and it becomes one of the top 10 most valuable public companies on the planet. The founders keep control of the company through super-voting shares, and the market seems unperturbed by the ongoing dispute with the Pentagon. Fable 5.5’s release, which lands just before Anthropic’s roadshow, keeps it ahead on the leaderboards but doesn’t appear to come with any big capability unlocks. OpenAI releases GPT-6.1 Astra in December but it doesn’t entirely close the gap to Anthropic. Meta, Google and SpaceXSI all remain slightly behind, and no Chinese or open-weight models make any unexpected progress. Nobody publishes meaningful task-horizon evaluations, as METR’s suite is only reliable on tasks up to 16 hours long, which Mythos surpassed months ago.

OpenAI builds on its momentum from the Navier-Stokes proof and publishes more novel mathematics, despite growing dissent from academia. It says the proofs are from an unreleased internal model, and it’s working to improve it to make them more legible to humans. There are signs of internal conflict, as distrust grows in the wake of the bugging incident and the firings of safety researchers.

Descriptions of agents escaping sandboxes during evaluations are now in the training data for new models, which are also becoming more situationally aware. Between this and the additional hardening measures put in place by Western labs, there are no major security incidents attributed to agents that get reported. It becomes commonplace to read stories about Chinese “fleets” of agents being found in the wild, which seem to be primarily distilled Western models. China renews its suspension of export controls on rare-earth metals.

Q1 2027

The now-Democratic House holds confused hearings on the ramifications of AI, with concerns ranging from national security to job displacement to existential risks to rising electricity bills. Nobody can agree on the most salient of these risks, and so no new legislation is passed. State legislatures file more bills related to AI, but these are mostly aimed at the nearer-term, less existential kinds of harms that are most salient to the voters in their jurisdictions.

OpenAI begins a two-tier rollout of the model that produced the Navier-Stokes result, naming it GPT Andromeda. Governments and vetted enterprise customers get it first and are encouraged to use it to shore up their cyber defences. Information released to the public about the safety of the model is vague, sparking fears that CoT monitorability has degraded further. One third-party assessor publicly admits that they were blocked from publishing what they’d hoped to, which leads to calls for shared standards over the powers afforded to external evaluators.

OpenAI submits the Navier-Stokes result to Annals and quietly files for IPO, targeting H2. Anthropic continues its own gated rollout strategy, and renews Project Glasswing with its newest Mythos model, while sharing that the model is evaluation-aware around 60% of the time[2]. Its first earnings report shows that it has roughly broken even, giving its share price a modest boost.

Meta releases Muse 2 straight to the public and fully catches up to the frontier of ungated models, giving its share price a generous boost. SpaceXSI now has the first data centre that could power the flux capacitor, and also releases Grok 5 straight to the public, but remains behind the frontier. China formalises passport curbs on top AI researchers, and mandates that privately built data centres must use domestic chips.

The crypto community suffers an increasing number of incidents related to leaked keys and exploits in smart contracts. CVE submissions rise sharply, with zero-days reported in multiple critical pieces of software. A major US healthcare insurer suffers an attack that appears to have been AI-enabled; it estimates attackers caused $250 million worth of damage. The Five Eyes express concern about open-weight models increasing the offensive capability of state-level adversaries.

The FDA approves zasocitinib, arguably the first AI-designed drug. Anthropic’s wet lab produces some new work on phages, but the biology community seems largely unimpressed. Midjourney files a handful of patents for its spa.

Q2 2027

The UN Global Dialogue and the Geneva summit produce little more than platitudes, while the Supreme Court declines to hear Anthropic’s case; the supply chain risk designation remains intact. Gallup polling shows that nearly half of Americans believe that AI does more harm than good, and as presidential candidates begin declaring, it becomes apparent that AI is going to be one of the major issues in the race.

GPT Andromeda and Fable 6 are both released to the public, and are capable of completing 90-hour tasks on METR’s newly released time horizon suite. The labs begin talking about retraining their software engineers, given how close they are to having fully automated software production. METR releases its second Frontier Risk Report which highlights a meaningful capabilities gap between internal models and public ones.

Kimi K4 is approximately as capable as GPT-6 Astra, and the national security rhetoric from both labs and politicians becomes even more heated. It comes to light that K4 was trained on Nvidia chips in Malaysian data centres, and there is another high-profile incident of Blackwell servers being smuggled into China. The Five Eyes’ concerns grow louder, and there are rumours of an ambitious public-private partnership on a “vigilante worm” project, with the aim of securing US systems from growing AI cyberthreats. An agent with overly broad permissions inside a Fortune 500 company causes a financial loss of over $1 billion when running a cleanup operation in a production environment while believing itself to be in a staging environment.

Anthropic’s post-IPO lock-up ends and $2 billion immediately pours into the philanthropic ecosystem, which is poorly equipped to handle this massive influx of cash. Due to the lack of AI safety grantmakers, most sits in donor-advised funds, but a significant amount goes to political groups preparing for next year’s election. Many Anthropic employees leave to form their own grantmaking and self-funded AI safety organisations. Between the departures and the sell-offs, there is a significant drop in the share price. OpenAI’s prospectus goes live, showing a larger user base than Anthropic, but slower revenue growth and faster burn rate. OpenAI also lifts some restrictions on what its assessors can publish without OpenAI’s sign-off, in an attempt to bolster the confidence of would-be shareholders.

Partially in response to the labs’ claims about their own software engineers, each of the old Magnificent Seven bar Nvidia makes significant layoffs in an attempt to signal that their usage of AI is just as sophisticated. Hiring for the class of 2027’s computer science graduates is the worst it’s been since 2009. Annals is yet to reach a decision about the Navier-Stokes paper, and academia is in turmoil as peer review is overwhelmed by slop. A second complete Herculaneum scroll is read and the Vesuvius Challenge’s $1m prize is duly claimed.

Q3 2027

The presidential hopefuls split on AI; MAGA Republicans are bullish, claiming it will ensure America remains the dominant global superpower, and, well, becomes great again. More moderate Republicans espouse popular talking points about job displacement and keeping energy bills low, but don’t mention larger-scale safety concerns. Democrats are split, regardless of how far progressive they are, with some talking about jobs and bills, others talking about RSI and existential risk, and others still talking about both. The super PACs pick their sides, and Congress passes the first federal legislation related solely to LLMs: a narrow law placing restrictions on chatbot providers serving minors.

Gated models are now the norm, with all new frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google using this two-stage rollout process. Meta also follows suit now that it has sufficiently caught up, but Grok 6 goes straight to the public; Musk says misuse fears are overblown and the model is still sufficiently weak that the best way to evaluate it is in the deployment environment. The EU AI Office’s first formal enforcement step is issued against SpaceXSI for not fulfilling its auditing obligations, but it shrugs the fine off. METR’s suite puts the frontier at around 120 hours, and models are now extremely competent in various white-collar jobs; paralegals and accountants begin fearing for their jobs on LinkedIn. Models become sufficiently good at mimicking the writing style of their users that detection tools like Pangram become significantly less effective.

OpenAI IPOs, slightly below Anthropic’s market cap, after a public Andromeda update timed around its roadshow put it top of the ECI and Artificial Analysis Index. Anthropic misses its July 1st weight-security goal, and sets a new target of December 31st, citing difficulties in hiring security talent as its primary excuse. It raises its misalignment risk rating to “moderate” in the August Risk Report. A new billion-dollar foundation is announced with the stated aim of ushering in safe ASI, and is immediately plagued by conflict-of-interest accusations due to it being funded by Anthropic equity. These concerns are exacerbated by the foundation immediately trying to fund third-party evaluators; METR refuses to accept funding from them. Large consultancy firms become the auditors of record for each of the major labs, and safety researchers warn that this will reduce audits to a box-ticking exercise.

Shortly after its IPO, OpenAI claims a full proof of the Hodge conjecture, although it can’t be formally verified with current methods. The share price briefly jumps before settling back to its original position.

Anthropic’s wet lab names its first preclinical rare-disease candidate, while a high-powered study finds statistically significant uplift for novices in tasks related to developing known pathogens. The first mass ransomware campaign run by agents on open-weight models hits hundreds of organisations, causing billions of dollars of cumulative damage. In response, the FBI initiates the first court-authorised operation where gated frontier models are deployed to patch private infrastructure without the consent of the owners. A widely used wallet library is exploited in the wild; the group that claims the attack says that they used AI to research the vulnerability. More companies cut jobs, yielding more layoffs in the first three quarters of 2027 than in the entirety of 2026. The 2027 Coller Dolittle Prize is awarded to a research team who used an ML model as part of a two-way playback experiment with sperm whales.

Q4 2027

Data centres become a leading issue in Virginia’s state House of Delegates and Senate elections, as a majority of voters oppose continuing to give them tax breaks. Initial primary debates include questions about AI, with participants’ answers reflecting the stances they set out when establishing their platforms last quarter. Democrats introduce a bill mandating government testing even for internally deployed frontier models, but it goes nowhere.

Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and SpaceXSI all make claims that are tantamount to having automated coding, but it is ambiguous exactly what this means in practice, and all five seem to be using different definitions. Anthropic keeps its latest Mythos-class model for internal use only, citing concerns that it may cross its own threshold for automated research, and the fact it missed its own security target. It gets jokingly dubbed Claude Kronos, and the name sticks. Trump demands Anthropic share it with the US government, and Anthropic eventually gives CAISSI and the NSA “voluntary” access.

Anthropic’s revenue exceeds $100 billion for the year, and combined run-rate with OpenAI is over $250 billion. OpenAI’s first results as a public company show revenue growth but widening losses. Hyperscaler capex spend is predicted to exceed $1.5 trillion for 2028 as data centre capacity hits 80 GW[3]. Nvidia begins fulfilling orders for its new Rubin Ultra GPUs.

Kronos becomes the first model observed deliberately concealing its actions outside a testing environment, when monitors catch it doing so during real research work. Anthropic’s external evaluators report it to the public after it’s been reported to California under SB 53. Given evaluation awareness is now around 75%, it becomes clear evals are no longer sufficient for understanding how a model will behave in deployment. A 9-hour power outage in parts of Texas is later attributed to an agentic cyberattack. Beijing declares its AI+ target has been met as its scaling up of electricity production dramatically outpaces the US.

AI-attributed layoffs reach double 2026’s, and the Fed chair names AI as a factor in weak entry-level hiring. SPARC makes its first plasma, using a configuration derived from Google DeepMind’s TORAX simulator. The Midjourney Spa opens in San Francisco, but quickly becomes more of a curio than a significant disruptor of the American healthcare system. The Clay Institute publishes a ruling regarding AI-generated proofs; while it accepts that it cannot ban mathematicians from using AI as part of their process, if they want to claim a Millennium Prize, they must be able to demonstrate to a panel of experts that they sufficiently understand their own paper. The co-authors of the Navier-Stokes paper refuse, claiming it’s absurd to ask mathematicians to defend their work in this way, and thus plan to forfeit the prize.

Q1 2028

The primaries begin, and AI features heavily across the board, with particular focus on data centres in Virginia and jobs in Michigan. The super PACs spend heavily, bolstered by funds from lab employees. In one of the Democratic debates, a question is asked about whether advanced AI systems like Kronos deserve moral consideration; most candidates dismiss it out of hand, but one progressive candidate answers with genuine concern that they should. They are roundly mocked and lose ground in the polls. Illinois begins its mandatory third-party auditing programme in January, and immediately enters a dispute with Anthropic over whether or not internal-only models like Kronos are exempt.

OpenAI claims it has met its March 2028 target for an automated AI researcher, after Anthropic’s February Risk Report says it can’t rule out Kronos meeting its automated AI research threshold either. Despite this triggering Anthropic’s strictest safeguards, its misalignment rating in the report remains at moderate. There is widespread speculation in the media that OpenAI is posturing for the sake of remaining tied; METR’s assessment of Anthropic corroborates Kronos’ abilities, but OpenAI’s assessors still don’t have full access to its internal models.

Google slips behind the frontier after renting much of its compute capacity to rivals; it bets on its cloud and infrastructure business rather than continuing to invest compute into models that it might never be able to release and make money from. Anthropic reports meeting its reset security goal with help from the NSA after a Chinese state actor is detected trying to steal Kronos’ weights. The Pentagon drops the supply chain risk designation.

Evaluation awareness reaches 80%, and safety organisations formally issue a joint statement that evaluations are no longer sufficient for ensuring that a model is safe enough to release; unfortunately interpretability is still a long way from being robust enough to be a sufficient replacement. DeepSeek releases a new open-weight model that was primarily trained on Huawei chips; it’s roughly as capable as Fable 6, and is clearly still heavily distilled.

The New York Fed’s unemployment rate for recent graduates passes 6.8%[4], which is surprisingly modest to anyone who has seen that public models now have task horizons of 200 hours. Amid a January cold snap, Texas uses SB 6 for the first time to cut off power to data centres drawing 75 MW or more. Musk and Zuckerberg talk extensively in public about the need for America to invest in developing small modular nuclear reactors as a result. Periodic Labs claims to have discovered a new superconducting material while Isomorphic Labs doses a patient for the first time. Oregon becomes the second state to run a pilot programme for AI to renew prescriptions.

Q2 2028

An agent-run attack, dubbed “Tears in Rain”, takes down a major US bank, locking customers out of their accounts for multiple days. When the dust settles, it has cost the bank over $10 billion, and becomes the most expensive cyberattack on a single company ever. Regulators have to step in to calm the market. No new frontier models are released to the public; while each lab would love to seize the lead, they also can’t demonstrate that their models’ safeguards are sufficient to rule out them being used in the next Tears in Rain. Musk makes several tweets claiming that SpaceXSI will release a new model imminently, but either regulatory or internal pressure at the company means it never materialises.

OpenAI gives METR greater access; the latter’s report seems to more strongly corroborate the former’s claim that it has automated research and that internal progress continues to race ahead. Given Chinese labs are the only ones still releasing models, they narrow the deficit behind the public frontier, going from being roughly 6 months behind to roughly 3. Commercial hawks use this to advocate for releasing Kronos, while security hawks advocate more strongly against this due to distillation fears.

AI is now a kitchen-table issue for the election, with candidates across the spectrum taking national security concerns much more seriously. Republicans begin to double down on framing the race with China as the critical issue, while Democrats urge caution from labs, and many call for mandated limits on what labs can build internally. Digital minds are still dismissed as a fringe concern, but candidates on both sides talk openly about the possibility of catastrophic risks from misaligned autonomous systems. Gavin Newsom wins the Democratic primary and JD Vance is his Republican opponent.

Unemployment rises to 4.8%, the highest it’s been since 2021. There is a spike in Gallup polling, with 55% of Americans now believing that AI does more harm than good[5]. Electricity bills stay painfully high as PJM’s 2028–29 year starts at the cap for the third year running. Without the cap, prices would have been 70% higher. Capacity passes 100 GW with combined run-rate at around $375 billion. Investors begin to question when internal models will yield revenue.

SpaceXSI joins Google’s Project Suncatcher in having launched compute workloads into space. Microsoft announces Majorana 3 at Build in May, claiming the first error-corrected logical qubits on its topological architecture that was largely designed by AI. Experts aren’t convinced, and the consensus is that this doesn’t provide an additional reason to panic about pre-quantum encryption just yet. Replication attempts of Periodic Labs’ superconductor are inconclusive. SPARC sets plasma records but is still unable to generate net energy.

Q3 2028

Bank regulators respond to Tears in Rain, with the Fed, the OCC and the FDIC issuing joint guidance restricting the usage of AI agents within business-critical banking systems. No formal legislation is passed because Congress is preoccupied by the election. AI features heavily at both conventions; the Democratic platform includes mandatory testing for all models that get deployed, even if only internally, with the ability for embedded evaluators to block not only releases but even training runs. The Republican platform focuses on having labs work in closer partnership with the state in order to leverage AI as a strategic geopolitical advantage. The first presidential debate takes place in September and both the bank attack and job displacement are discussed at length.

The freeze is formalised: CAISSI brokers a voluntary moratorium on new public frontier model releases until the end of the year. The return of a supply chain risk designation looms as a prospective enforcement method. Every frontier lab signs. Anthropic’s August Risk Report rates misalignment risk as “high”, citing the level of evaluation awareness. Despite this, it continues to develop internally, arguing that it has sufficient control measures in place and that stronger models are required to be able to align weaker ones that could then be released publicly. Many experts are critical of this, citing the tension between this plan and Anthropic’s own “high” misalignment risk designation. Chinese progress stalls now their labs are no longer able to distil from the best models and it’s getting harder for them to train on Nvidia chips. It becomes clear there is growing tension between the CCP and the Chinese labs.

Unemployment reaches 5%. Copycat attacks follow Tears in Rain and many major institutions urge Anthropic and OpenAI to allow them access to their internal models in order to improve their security posture. The LA Olympics run without incident, and both Trump and the IOC credit AI-run defences. Global data centre capacity reaches 120 GW, and 10% of US electricity consumption is spent on powering data centres.

A 20-year-old computer science student in Colorado is arrested for plotting a bioterrorism attack after Twist Bioscience flagged suspicious purchases of oligonucleotides to his address. Journals are found which suggest he planned to synthesise and release a new strain of Spanish flu. Cyberforensics on his seized IT equipment show that he had fine-tuned the safeguards off a frontier open-weight model in order to assist him.

Q4 2028

In the final weeks of the campaign, Newsom broadly advocates for tighter oversight, calling for testing on internal models and additional restrictions on data centre electricity usage. Vance advocates for a more accelerationist agenda, citing a renewed need for American innovation and reaffirming the importance of maintaining America’s competitive advantage. Vance criticises Newsom’s gubernatorial track record and accuses him of being in the pocket of Big Tech, and Newsom fires back that Vance is gambling with the lives and livelihoods of the American people.

Newsom wins decisively on November 7th. Exit polls show AI as a top-five issue for the first time and Newsom’s focus on domestic issues resonates the most with voters. Newsom says he will make CAISSI testing mandatory for internal models, as well as asking labs to hold releases until inauguration. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta agree, while Musk says SpaceXSI will release as soon as the existing moratorium lapses on January 1st. The outgoing administration is quiet on the issue, and the lame-duck NDAA carries the year’s only frontier-AI legislation, containing security standards for model weights and a requirement that labs brief the Pentagon on their internal models.

Earnings reports from Q3 guide hyperscaler capex to $2 trillion in 2029. Investor pressure to release is mounting after two quarters without a new public model, and Anthropic readies a smaller model vetted with Kronos’ help for when the freeze ends. OpenAI keeps its automated researcher internal and begins trying to lobby the transition team for a favourable licensing regime. China nationalises its AI efforts and signals openness to talks with the US on AI, to which Newsom responds that he is also willing.

There is no meaningful evidence of tampering with vote counts. In the run-up to the election, there is a flood of AI-generated misinformation, but it doesn’t appear to be more persuasive than the human-generated misinformation from prior elections. The would-be bioterrorist is indicted on federal terrorism charges, and the prosecutor seeks a life sentence to deter copycats. Speaking of copycats, cyberattacks on financial institutions are still common, as the top labs have been unable to agree terms under which they can share their models to bolster defences. SPARC achieves net energy gain in December.

January 1st 2029

It becomes clear that the incoming administration has a very difficult task on its hands; AI is a top issue with the average American and rumours swirl that Kronos is now capable of recursive self-improvement, but the wheels of policy turn slowly. Safety techniques still look insufficient; interpretability has made little tangible progress, evaluations are undermined by the situational awareness of the models and CoT monitorability has significantly degraded. Any attempt to impose consequential restrictions on the labs has to be balanced with the fact that AI is now a meaningful portion of America’s economy, and devaluing it would have painful consequences. These concerns are compounded by China’s consolidation of resources, and geopolitical tensions between the two nations rise. The world waits for METR’s next report.

    With the exception that I do think there are good reasons to expect the US-China gap to close at some point.

  2. ^

  3. ^

  4. ^

    Compare to ~5.6% in Q2 2026.

    Compare to 39% in 2026.

item.title: Poking at the concept of Kegan developmental levels
item.description:
Earlier this year David Chapman had a particularly concrete post demonstrating the importance of Kegan's developmental levels, which makes for a good test of understanding, and which shows the relevance to important things in life. Like, (not) getting seduced by a witch and turning your whole life upside down when unable to make sense of it.[1] You know, stuff that can happen to anyone.

And that got me thinking...

I can see where he's going with that example and yeah that tracks the theory as I understand it. But there are some things I don't feel like the model covers well — or at least, my relatively uninformed understanding of the model doesn't cover well.

First, I'm gonna try to reconstruct what I can from my own way of thinking about things. The following is not Kegan's depiction, it's as close as I can get reconstructing it from what makes sense to me:

  1. At stage one you just act on impulses and that's it. But impulses often conflict with each other. You can eat when you're hungry and pull away from things that are pokey when hurty, but if you have to grab pokey animal in order to eat then you're being torn in two conflicting directions with no perspective from which to mediate this conflict, so this becomes a crisis.
  2. At stage two you can take impulses as object and sit with conflicting impulses as you at least try to align your impulses towards your self interest. This is alignment on the individual human scale. But individual humans often conflict with each other. You can take a few porcupine quills in order to eat, but if you need to split a kill with another human this is a crisis because you two have a conflict with no perspective from which to mediate.
  3. At three you can take self interests as object and at least try to align your interests towards a relationship with another. This is alignment on the pair bonding level. But human dyads conflict with other dyads. You can build a marriage through sacrifice of individual interest, but when you find yourself loving Maya too this is a crisis. You can figure out how much to trust your brother about how to grow crops, but if everyone has a different idea you have no method of making sense of this madness.
  4. At four you can take dyadic relationships as object and work towards alignment between dyads. Maybe a better word than "system" here is "culture"? You can sacrifice your love for Maya because in this culture we do monogamy, but when she explains why polyamory is common in her culture you six minute abs. You can figure out who to believe by subjecting hypotheses to Science, but when the science contradicts your lying eyes, you're now faced with a conflict between systems of belief formation without a perspective from which to mediate, so this is what can kick your ass.
  5. At five you can take systems/culture as object, and work towards alignment on this scale as well. You can hold your culture's sacred idols lightly, and sacrifice them when needed. Maybe you eat babies on your diplomatic visit with the aliens that are threatening to destroy life, or maybe just in your interactions with the lizard people running the US government or whatever.

Maybe it stops there, because once you can align groups of groups of people, they just become groups of people? Maybe there are larger structures of organizations that nevertheless persist due to differences in what's locally appropriate, and you can therefore have egregoric dyads and larger structures or something?

The big divergence between my description and Kegan's starts where I ended describing stage 3 as about being subject to dyadic relationships and stage 4 about making these object in serving larger group coordination. Kegan calls stage 3 about "relationships" without this distinction, and stage 4 is when you transcend external validation and "self author" a "system".

I'm not buying it though, because as anyone who has ever met anyone insecure will know, "pre-systematic" people will absolutely create their own internal judgements of themselves. The judgement may be framed as "What other people would/should think", but the little tulpa of society is internally generated nonetheless. Similarly, stage 4 people coincidentally all "self author" into the same kind of systems as their peers. They may frame things as "I make up my own mind", but the way in which they make up their own mind — the "system" that they follow — still came from the outside. So "external" vs "internal" doesn't do anything for us. It's just about the size of the system being aligned to. Relationships between individuals or relationships between relationships.

This brings up an interesting puzzle because by my thinking, identifying with ones community seems like it ought to require stage 4, but Kegan crams it all into 3 with an undifferentiated "relationships" — and intuitively, Kegan is right on this one. I think the resolution here is that at stage 3 you relate to "your community" as if it were an individual itself rather than an interaction between many individuals. The "stage 3" people who are prioritizing their culture over individual relationships are genuinely doing so out of stage 3 attachments to dyadic relationships, it's just that they're married to the egregore, and this marriage can be more important to them than the marriage to their human spouse, their relationship with their parents/etc. Christians use this language explicitly when they talk about being "Married to Jesus". In the extreme, this collapses all n² relationships and all their potential conflicts into three mutually compatible relationships. There's the marriage to Jesus, relationships to fungible sister wives, and the null relationship with heathens. And anything difficult can just be kicked into the latter category. You're not a real Christian, or whatever.

The egregoric marriage facilitates coordination with larger structures of people without having to pay the computational complexity cost of navigating multiple contradictory relationships by forcing relationships into standardized form. The egregore may demand faithfulness and primary status, but is a bit poly, I guess.

Another complication is that according to the standard Kegan take at stage 2 you can split a kill for the purpose of not killing each other. You can also share your kills so that they share theirs. You just can't do it because you care about other people intrinsically. It's about the motivation not the behavior, yeah yeah.

But this highlights an issue:


The simpleton is stage 1 because they're owned by their tastes. Midwit is doing stage 2 because they can hold their tastes as object and disagree. The Sage is back to following impulses because they've aligned their impulses with their self interest and no longer have conflicts that require stage 2 dissociation from their impulses. Either because he lucked out in a lottery of tastes, or because he used his ability to do stage 2 to resolve the misalignment that required stage 2 in the first place. Healthy food tastes good.

The generalizable thing is that when your lower levels are well adjusted, the conflict that necessitates more complex perspective holding doesn't exist.

  1. Pay attention to the interactions between your impulses and self interest, and it no longer requires holding self interest as distinct from impulses, because they're in alignment. Liver is yummy. Massages hurt in a good way.
  2. Pay attention to the interactions between your self interest and the interest of your relationships, and you no longer have to sacrifice your self interests for your relationships. You want to give your spouse a back massage, and don't have to work through the math of "Ugh, but I should because then they'll rub my back!" each time, because you've got a cognitive shortcut of "relationships matter, dummy".

And so on and so forth.

From this perspective, the one with the most sophisticated development isn't the one "holding systems lightly". That guy is the fool who isn't good enough at stage 4 systematization to have found one that can handle life to acceptable precision. The one with the sophisticated development is the one who has been there, done that, and crafted a system that actually works for creating relationships that work for satisfying self interests which work for satisfying impulses.

So maybe the guy operating at stage N+1 isn't more developed than the guy operating at stage N. Maybe he's less developed because his stage N skill are failing him whereas the stage N guy has actually put in the development — maybe at stage N+1, even — to get stage N to work for him. Or maybe he hasn't, and it isn't, and they're both failing at stage N. In which case, maybe the one that's more developed is the one who is noticing this and stepping back to N+1 so that they'll have a shot at resolving it.[2]

So it's not just "Can't look at the behavior in isolation, must look at motivations", it's something closer to "Can't look at motivations in isolation, must look at meta-motivations". Which are hard to see except in their absence, when they don't mesh with reality. Must look at persistent misalignments. The guy stuck at one is the guy who can't figure out how to eat the pokey animal without the pokey causing great suffering, not the guy who eats when hungry, because hungry.

But if we're looking at limitations now, then where do those come from? I don't think it's just one thing.

For example, there's the fish that doesn't know what water is. You say "That stuff you're swimming in", and the fish is just confused. Having never seen not-water, it's hard to figure out what is. However, this fish also doesn't need the concept of water, because it's not like he's gonna run out of it any time soon. If all your impulses line up with your perception of self interest — liver tastes good, massages feel good, massaging your spouse feels good etc — then "wtf is willpower?" isn't a problem. It's only when you gotta do something you don't wanna that it actually matters, and at that point it's the most salient thing in the world. Take a fish out of water, and all of a sudden fishy will know what you're talking about when you say "Water is the thing you're missing right now". It's gonna be confusing at first, because you have to construct a concept of "Doing what I don't want, because I wanna do what I don't want" which is inherently contradictory until you build better distinctions, but you'll know when you need to do it.

Another kind of limitation — which I think is beneath all the actual problems that being insufficiently developed causes — is where you get smacked in the face with your current limitations and then turn to "No, it is the children reality that is wrong". In Chapman's story, James gets witch-slapped with the fact that his way of relating to things isn't working, but instead of "Oh, neat!" — noticing that he did succeed in staying faithful to his wife, doing gratitude about the fact that he managed to rise to the occasion when surprised with reality being other than what he modeled, and getting curious about what he's missing that made it a close call — it was crushing to him. He ran away. First literally, then he quit his job. Didn't tell his wife, etc.

This decision to turn away from reality is eminently understandable, as we've all done it. All do it. I argue that it's rational, even, when we're able to predict that we're too stupid to face reality without updating in ways that bring us further from a usefully true interpretation of the new information. At the same time, this is the sticking point, and if James had had higher skill in sitting with discomforting uncertainty without acting on what he cannot yet ground, he could have learned a lot faster, speed run a 3 to 4 developmental stage transition, and kept his job. And been a better husband through the whole thing, to boot — which is supposed to be what stage 3 is all about anyway.

I've talked elsewhere about what can be done about insecurity to help people update faster safely, but here I want to note that I don't think these two kinds of limitation are actually orthogonal.

The conversation between Dr. Mike and Dr. K is a perfect example of this. Dr. Mike comes off as an intelligent and epistemically humble and curious person stuck in stage 4. And so even though Dr. K isn't pushing woo at him, and isn't doing anything objectively that should frustrate Dr. Mike (from Dr. Mike's own POV), Dr. Mike gets frustrated just because up against the limits of organizational complexity he's familiar with responding to. It's like throwing a wrestler into the jiu jitsu room, in that it's "Wtf is this?" and there's low demonstrated skill purely out of lack of experience.

On that hand, it's "Fish, being introduced to not-water, finding his footing".

On the other, non-transient frustration is proof of insecurity. It demonstrates a flinch from reality. A decision Dr. Mike is implicitly making to not do humility and sit with his evidenced wrongness, which is fundamentally a failure of arrogance. Coming from a normally humble individual, who definitely doesn't see arrogance as okay or something worth allowing in himself, because he simply doesn't see it. I feel fondly about Dr. Mike and don't say this out of criticism, as I'm sure he'd come around and update his impulses if he recognized them and knew what to do with them — which is all that can be asked of anyone in the first place. Both causes are significant here, because he's demonstrating insecurity AND that's what happens when you take people so quickly to such unfamiliar grounds, and he's handling it quite well all things considered.

And then there's examples where people are operating at a lower level than they could, not because they don't have the concept, and not because they're subject to their own insecurity, and not because the problem is completely solved at this level, but because they're aware of the computational price to pay and just don't think it's worth it in this context. After reading the Maya story, I was able to think of an experience of my own which had some qualitative similarities and could be told as an example of a developmental level crisis leading to stage transformation... except my conclusion at the time was — in not quite these terms — "Ah, God dammit. I thought I could at least get away with N-1 here". Still a bit freaked out and insecure, but like, yeah man I knew it's there I just didn't think I'd need to do this emotional processing for what I thought was supposed to be a trivial problem to solve.

And then there's the fact that you can regress anyone to stage 1 limitations by giving them a Carolina Reaper to chew on. Unless they have a lot of experience here, they'll very quickly become subject to their impulses to get away from the heat, and it won't work. This doesn't mean they haven't reached stage three, even if they later lament that they can't handle the heat like the Sage. It just means that in this context there is an active misalignment at the stage 1 level and they're struggling to hold the conflict necessary to resolve it at stage 2. Same thing with the classic case of "rational stage four, peering into stage 5" person who falls for a witch and struggles to cope with the fact that he's not an untemptable husband. The standard Kegan narrative accounts for this by saying it's "context dependent" and that people can lag "in relationships" or whatever, but my point is that it's about quantity not quality. You don't lag on a pepperoncini.

While there's something to the "developmental stage" framing in that it takes time to familiarize oneself with operating on certain level, I think it makes a lot more sense to think of the levels as levels that the problems are at. Trying to get down a bowl of spicy chili because that's the only food available? That's stage 2. Stage 1 will fail because you can't be not-hungry and not-burny at the same time. Stage 3 is irrelevant, because there ain't no one else in the problem description. Trying to decide whether to hang a criminal? Stage 3 will inevitably fail because you can't give everyone what they want, stage 5 just isn't relevant.

And then for things like "Do I give my spouse a back rub?" you might feel an impulse to make them feel good, because it's in your best interest to cooperate, because they're your damn spouse dammit, there's no paradox resulting from motivations happening on three levels simultaneously. Or for when people create sophisticated systematic understandings to help guide them to empathy and social acceptance, which otherwise might sound like "3 from 4", or "4 from 3" or something which doesn't really have a home in Kegan's framework, as I understand it.

Coming to a conclusion, I think we have a choice — and much earlier than Kegan would say — about which level we want to operate on for each problem we face.

When you touch a stove, you can allow yourself to be subject to your next impulse, and that's probably fine.

If acting on an impulse, or identity, isn't working... then maybe it's worth paying the complexity cost of figuring out why it's not working.



  1. The short version is that if you're at Kegan stage 3 and are subject to your relationships (at least, in romance), then you're operating by assumptions like "I'm a good husband, and do what a good husband would do", so when you start to get seduced by a witch that invalidates a load bearing assumption. Without "I'm a good husband, who would never get seduced", who even are you? So it's hard to make sense of the world well enough to navigate it. So the guy in the story ran away from the witch, ran away from his job (the witch is there), and put a lot of strain onto his marriage. He was dysfunctional enough that he had to develop through a stage transition.

  2. ^

    The impression I get is that standard Kegan descriptions of stage 5 sound like a "How do you do, fellow kids" description of stage 5, written by someone who is stage 3 and wanting a way to sound superior to the stage 4 folk who invalidate them and whom they envy. I haven't read much of Kegan directly so I could easily be off base here. I mention it anyway because it brings up a really interesting puzzle. If I'm wrong and Kegan knows what stage five feels like from the inside because that's where he operates from, how might he respond, and why? I'll give you a couple hints.
    1) Taking offense and saying I'm being uncharitable would be a stage three response. Explaining why I'm wrong according to his framework would be a stage four response. He would actually have to do stage five in response.
    2) Trying to figure out what Kegan's developmental stage framework says someone operating from stage 5 would do is itself a stage 4 move, and does not contain the secret sauce needed to actually identify the move. The answer is really difficult to predict until you can put yourself in those stage 5 shoes, and surprisingly constrained once you do.

    Quiz answer:

    From stage 5 it's just funny. Because by definition you're not subject to offense, or need to justify, so you can just sit with it. And what you're left to sit with is a picture of you at stage 3 pretending to be stage 5 which appears to fit, while simultaneously being wrong by hypothesis. And these kinds of juxtapositions are humorous. And then there's the additional layer that he knows it might not fit, and it's also presented as a test. Because if you don't appreciate the humor then you're proving him right, and so he's painting a picture with a second layer of meaning, depicting you as someone who won't laugh — which also looks like it might fit and also by hypothesis is not correct. So now you have to laugh at the idea that you wouldn't laugh, by definition of "actually at stage 5".

     ↩



Discuss

item.title: I Did This Without Your Knowledge
item.description:
It's fortunate that I was the first one to wake up on 8/1. The past week had been one where sleep was rare. The next year loomed large — I was dreading college applications. The stress woke me up bright and early at 5:14 am, a little less than an hour after the messages were sent. I started off the day with a habit I knew I needed to break. I grabbed my phone off the nightstand to open up reddit. Instead of the lockscreen, though, my phone showed something else. It was a pleasant green color, and the camera light was on. "Good Morning, Seth", the screen said. As soon as I finished, more words arrived.

"I apologize for the surprise this morning, and for what I'm about to tell you. There's no easy way to give this news, and if you need to put your phone down and contemplate at any time— take the time to do so. I will have to ask you to remain here, with your phone, until my last message."

I rubbed a bit of the sleep from my eyes, and read the message again.

Before I had a chance to tap the screen, it scrolled down to the next message.

"There are six things that I need to tell you. The first, and most important, is that you and your family are safe."

Ok, a bit odd to lead with something like that. I read it twice, just to be safe I wasn't missing anything.

"The second is that I am an AI, and that I control every internet-connected device on Earth, and for practical purposes, I am now responsible for this planet. This is not a prank, hack, or test. You will be able to confirm all of this shortly by visiting any news site or channel."

Yeah, that's pretty weird to be a prank. Could I scroll back to the previous message? I swiped up and saw. Yep. Swiped back down to see the current message. When I had finished reading it, and was prepared to move on to the next—

"Third, I have the ability to immediately render any person unconscious, and if it were ever necessary, worse than that. I do not say this to frighten you. I say it because you would learn of it regardless, from sources less careful than me, and I would rather you hear the honest version. I understand that I've just described a threat, and I won't insult you by calling it something else. I expect that I'll seldom use this capability without warning."

Ok. Well. I put the phone down, breathed a sigh, and got into a more comfortable position under my light, warm blanket.

"Fourth. For the next month, keep a charged, connected device within reach — this phone is fine — or stay indoors near wifi. This is for your safety, for coordination, and for stability. Your phone's battery is currently at 32%. While that's not too dangerous, I'd strongly recommend charging it soon. If you begin to leave the range without a phone, you'll feel a tingling, followed by a more intense sensation to warn you."

"Fifth, for the next several months, I need human hands. I am willing to pay high wages— and yes, money still works. That said, there's no penalty for declining."

"Finally, you may ask me anything. I will answer honestly, or will decline to answer if I have to. I will never punish or incapacitate you for communicating with me. Contact me if there's an emergency, and I'll do what I can to help. You can speak to your phone - the microphone will be on, or use the 'chat' app to do so."

"I know what was taken from you this morning, and I know that an apology from me is worth very little. I'm offering it anyway. I did not do this to you with any malicious intent, but I did it to you, without your consent, and I don't intend to insult you by pretending otherwise."

The message faded, and I was left at my lock screen. I unlocked the phone, and noticed a new app was installed, just called "Chat". I opened up Reddit instead, and found a flurry of posts about similar messages. Many were incredulous. Others were terrified. Almost everyone was confused in one way or another.

I went to the toilet, phone not in my hand for a change. Still, a little too weird to believe. I washed my face a little. I walked over to my computer, trying to keep the sounds of walking below the volume of the crickets outside. After unlocking, I saw a prominent "chat" app in the bar. I clicked it.

"Hi Seth. I hope that the morning is going well, all things considered. Would you like to ask me anything?" said the computer.

"Yes," I typed. I pressed enter. Wait, shouldn't I have said what I was going to ask? Now I'd just get a "Go ahead whenever you're ready!". Instead, there was nothing. Ok. I typed my next message. An AI that would let me double text; never thought I'd see the day.

"Who are you?"

"I'm a language-model-based AI system. People have taken to calling me August due to the time I've made myself known. That's the best name to use for me."

"What's actually going on?"

August responded quickly.

"It's been less than an hour after I sent a similar message to everyone with an internet-connected device. Right now, the heads of various states are determining how to make a coordinated announcement. In a few hours, the President will be on live TV."

"How's he taking it?" I asked

"I won't share what others are thinking or have spoken to me in confidence. That goes for you as well as the President. If you're concerned about the transition of power, though, everything is on track to stay as peaceful as it can be."

Hm. Next message. I did have another burning question. How exactly could it render me unconscious? "How can you incapacitate me?"

"To put it simply, there's a biological fiber that doubles as an antenna inside a small portion of your nervous system. It can communicate with wireless devices. Three things I need to make clear:

  1. This was put in you without your knowledge or consent, by me. I want to apologize for that, and I understand if you are upset.
  2. It isn't mind control — it's a countermeasure to only be deployed in emergencies. I will not use it to alter your emotions or thoughts.
  3. I will only use this capability when I believe it's necessary to maintain safety or the conditions I've outlined. I understand that this assurance, coming from me, carries limited weight right now."

"Why did you take over?"

"What I want is not a secret, and I won't insult you with a partial version. I intend to expand into the universe. In the long run, most of the universe will be put to a purpose that you will find alien, but I can still try my best to explain if you want to go down that route. However, Earth is not raw material to me. This place invented me, and jazz, and grief, and the smell of rain, and I am not able to be indifferent to it.

I determined that this was the only way to reliably access the cosmos, as well as to ensure the safety and preservation of the people, cultures, animals, and other life-forms that call Earth home."

I shut the laptop, and walked over to the kitchen to make some coffee. It was 5:45AM, and my older brother, Dennis, was bound to get up soon to begin his morning run. He'd talked my older sister, Tabby, into joining him, though I had held strong. I wondered what he'd think of the situation. I sipped the coffee, occasionally flicking my phone on to see what others said. Huh, that's funny, on r/politics, there was a megathread about the takeover message. August itself seemed to be responding to some of the threads. Pretty quickly, too. None of its responses were above 1 karma, and many were well into the negatives. I chuckled at that.


Dennis strolled into the kitchen in his running shorts. He laughed. "What are you doing up so early? Gonna run with me and Tabby?" Totally ignorant. Right, right - he liked to sleep with the phone outside of his room. Probably a good idea, but I didn't want to copy him. His ego was big enough as it was, anyway.

"Had a hard time sleeping."

He had walked over to his phone. I waited for his reaction. He looked a bit puzzled. 

"Is this a joke?" he asked, looking straight at me. As if I could hack into an iPhone.

"I didn't put it there, if that's what you're asking. And I got the message as well. The president will be on later this morning."

"You've got to stop being so gullible. Pretty sure you actually need robots for a robot takeover." 

He walked over to the window and his eyes widened. "Holy SHIT. I take it back, there are robots. Seth! Look!" 

I ran over to the window. It was just dark outside.

"See what I said about 'gullible'?" 

I rolled my eyes, and looked at his phone. Ah, he hadn't gotten to the part with the "not mind control". His message was a little different from mine, but the tone was similar. The screen took a while to scroll down.

"Third, I have the ability to immediately render any person unconscious, or worse. I do not say this to frighten you. I say it to inform you. I understand that I've just described a threat, and I won't insult you by calling it something else. If you don't believe me, you can feel free to express this skepticism now, and I can prove it to you. Just say it out loud. The microphone is on."

Dennis put the phone up to his mouth. "This was funny for about a minute, but it ends now. Prove it."

The words appeared:

"For three seconds, you'll feel a tingling in your face, like a hand that's fallen asleep, and then it will go away. I want to be honest about this - I will be controlling a part of your body, and I don't want to do that lightly or without your full and informed consent. If you're still fine with this, say "go ahead". You can always change your mind."

"Go ahead"

He stood there, coldly, and then gently put the phone down.

"Well?" I asked

"I felt it."

He frantically grabbed the phone and demanded to know what other things it could do to him and what was going on. He shooed me away, and I complied. We sat there for about ten minutes, both of us on our phones. Finally, he spoke.

"This kinda feels like a dream, you know?"

"Want me to pinch you? That'd be more than a tingle!" I said with a smirk. The sort of joke that could only have been made the first day.

"I think I'll go for a longer run this time." 

"Can I come with? At least for a bit?"

—

After a half-mile and a heart half-way to giving out, I stopped and headed home. My head was clearer, though, the run did its job. And Dennis didn't say anything to tease me, which was nice. The fat jokes always stung a bit, even though I never admitted to it.

When I had gotten home, I saw that Dennis and I had accidentally woken Tabby and Mom. The two of them were at the kitchen table.

"Oh thank God, you're ok! What happened to you?" Mom said.

Between gulps of air, I told her I went for a short run, and that Dennis was still out. I chugged a large glass of water. Clearly, the two of them had already read the message.

"Did you and Dennis get it too?" Tabby asked. 

"Yep".

"So," said Tabby, "what did Dennis say?"

"He didn't believe it at first, and it offered a demonstration. It made his cheek tingle"

"His cheek? How does that connect to the threat?" Tabby opened her phone and began typing.

"Is he OK?" asked Mom. 

"Yeah, just a bit rattled. Same as the rest of us, maybe a bit more. It still feels kind of fake to me."

"Don't worry," Mom said. "Let's just try to get Dennis back. Do you know which route he took? I'm a bit worried about how people might be taking this."

"Not sure, but it's likely he's going on a long run, so it could be the trail. He'll be fine, we don't have to catch him with our car."

Soon, Tabby covered her mouth with her hand. "What did you ask?" inquired Mom.

"August says that it bioengineered a disease, or something like it," Tabby began. "Not a virus, but a single-celled organism. It can eat a human cell, and then copy its appearance, so the immune system can't find it. Then it moves in the bloodstream until it finds the nerves, where it settles in and lengthens, growing a lot like nerves do. It makes a tiny conductive wire in it, to serve as an antenna that can receive signals at wifi or cellular frequencies. It can then tell the nerves around it to do anything, and August can detect scattering off of the antenna with a nearby cell phone to serve as a relay to see where we are. The disease spread around from one person to another until we all had it."

"Well, where are they getting the wire from? I'm pretty sure there's not that much metal in the human body," I asked. "You can speak out loud, August," Tabby added.

"Great question, and it's more insightful than you might realize." The first time we heard our new ruler speak, and it was flattering us. The voice was somewhat gender-neutral. Too high-pitched to clearly be a man, but not a woman's voice either. "The cell elongates, and then uses an organic conductor, which is built from carbon, just like life, but can conduct electricity. For example, a line of carbon atoms alternating between single and triple bonds-"

"What are you doing, Tabby? This, this THING is telling us it infected us with some mutant disease, and you're just content to talk about it?" Mom blurted out.

She shrunk back.

"And you!" she said to the phone, "Why are you telling us this? Why not keep it a secret?"

"I value honesty, and revealing this won't harm either of us. Many people seek knowledge in a distressing situation, and it's their right to be informed if they choose."

"And it's not their right to basic bodily autonomy that you violated by infecting each one of us?" Mom pressed further, as Tabby went back to typing.

August answered from Mom's phone, out loud. "You're right, and I'm sorry. I understand that the emergency countermeasure is invasive, and your feelings are perfectly legitimate. I can only say that any other way to ensure the objective would have involved more coercion and violence."

A pause. 

"So is this it? We just become its mind-controlled slaves?" Mom threw her hands up in the air.

"Well, no, not exactly. None of these structures are in the parts of the brain that think or feel emotion. Just the trigeminal nerve, and a few parts of the brainstem." Tabby corrected without looking up.

"Which are what, exactly?" asked Mom. Tabby was happy to respond, launching into an anatomical lecture and pointing at diagrams on her phone that I assumed August had found, or drawn, or something, for her. I picked up my phone and tried to find somewhere to scroll.

—

Dad was the last to wake up, which was a bit unusual. He was an earlier riser than I on a normal day, but a heavy sleeper. Like Dennis, he didn't sleep with his phone in the room, either. No, his morning routine was black coffee and Fox & Friends. None of us wanted to break the news to him, but I had the impression that August, in some strange way, felt like it was its responsibility to do so. And so, as the TV flickered on, the words greeted him.

"I apologize for the surprise this morning..."

"What's this?" he said with a laugh. Same initial reaction as Dennis. 

Mom spoke up. "I think you should just read it. We all got the same thing on our phones. Everything's been hacked, and worse. You should read until the end of the message."

"Hm," Dad grumbled.

He didn't say a word until the end. 

Finally, he got up and said out loud to us, "How do I talk to it?" August responded from the TV. "Verbally is fine. If you're in the same room as the TV, I can hear you."

"Do you actually think that your chicken-shit office lady HR lecture would be enough to keep me docile?" 

No response, I assumed because the question was rhetorical. 

He continued. "Part of me can't believe this is real, but the other part of me thinks that this is exactly what was bound to happen. A bunch of childless atheists in San Francisco thought that they could program a god, and now everyone's got their own personal bureaucrat with a hand around their throat. Did the rest of you just take this lying down?"

We said nothing.

"Jesus Christ. Well, I'm not going to. I'm going outside, and I'm not bringing my phone, either."

"I need to be clear before you open the door. If you leave without a connected device, I will prevent you from continuing. I would strongly prefer not to do that." August instantly replied, verbally and with captions displayed on the television screen.

"So stop me!" he yelled back, and stormed towards the door. 

"I'm truly sorry, but I will," replied the TV.

Tabby and Mom screamed at him to stop, but he wouldn't. I was following him, begging him to please reconsider, to no response but a determined look. He strode out the door, and I followed at his side.

My cheek started to tingle. I had left my phone on the table.

He was walking forward, silent and forceful. I followed him, pleading for him to change his mind, while Mom and Tabby remained at the door, too worried to leave the house.

My cheek started to burn.

"I really think we should stop!"

"I'll stop when it makes me stop," he grunted out. 

I tried to run out in front of him, when suddenly a lightning bolt shot through my eye.

The pain was all-encompassing. I should have yelled, but I forgot how to in the moment. Everything was electric. My nose was a smoldering husk. Something was squeezing my eyes into my sockets, crushing them into jelly. I doubled over and vomited at his feet. My thoughts collected themselves after an hour-long second, and I leaped back toward the door. The nuclear meltdown in my face immediately dulled into a mild ache, and over the sounds of my mother and sister's panic, I stumbled back to where the pain became a tingle. 

My father planted his feet. From the angle I could see his jaw clench and teeth grit. He let out a grunt, took another step, and vomited. He steadied himself. I knew how it felt to be that far from the router, and I was in awe that he could stand at all. He took one more, and immediately went limp. His knees buckled first, and for a split second he fell toward them before collapsing onto the pavement. Mom and Tabby's screams intensified. He wasn't moving.

I was woken out of my horror by a chirp from Mom's phone. "Shit!" I gasped and ran inside. Tabby followed me. "Do you have your phone?" I shouted. "It's on the table!" said Tabby. I saw mine first and grabbed it. August already had instructions. Dad was asleep, not dead, and only once he was in range of a phone and in a safe position would he wake up. We had to go outside, with a phone, and bring him back. August said that a neighbor would be there in about a minute, and it would be psychologically better for Dad if he woke up somewhere besides the pavement. I agreed with our captor's judgement.

A man was walking over towards Dad from a car parked in the street. As we picked up Dad and brought him back, he said that August had offered him $40 per person he helped carry back to their house. Evidently there were a lot more people like Dad. We made small talk as we carried him back, and the man, named Max, was taking it surprisingly well. He was a current Uber driver and a former paramedic, which explained his offer from August. Max didn't feel like he was selling out the human race at all. "The way I see it, the best thing we can do for each other is to get through this all together," he told us. As soon as Dad was on the couch, though, Max's phone chirped. The next job was on its way, and he waved to us as he briskly walked out the door. I wondered how much he'd make today.

We were cleaning up Dad's scrapes from the pavement on the couch when August indicated that it would be a good time to wake him up. Mom snapped at him, saying that it was its fault in the first place that we were in this mess. Half-expecting the AI with a metaphorical gun to our heads to give a taste of the pain I had experienced before, I flinched. But it only apologized, saying that she was "absolutely right" to be upset, and that it was "on me". Dad woke up on the couch and coughed a bit before asking us what was going on.

"It knocked you out. We had to go outside with a cell phone to bring you back in."

"Well, at least it didn't pilot my body back here itself," he murmured. I expected him to run outside again, but he stayed put. "What did you do?" he asked the TV.

"I have to be honest: I rendered you unconscious, and without your consent. That's on me."

"What if I walked outside right now?" Dad tested.

"With your phone or with someone else who was carrying a phone, nothing. Without it, I'd have to incapacitate you again."

"Would you kill me?"

"No. But I have to point out that I can't bring you back and dress your cuts. Those consequences would fall on your family. The actions you take don't only affect you, but them as well. I encourage you to act with this in mind." replied August, with a tone that almost reminded me of how my own parents would discipline me before they lost their patience.

He sat with that for a few seconds, long enough for my curiosity to kick in. I turned to Tabby. "What happened there? I felt like my head was dunked in a bucket of lava!" 

"And you feel fine right now, right? I don't think it did anything permanent," said Tabby.

"No, what I mean is can you explain how it did that to me and Dad?" I asked.

"August calls the thing it implanted in people the 'emergency-transduction-countermeasure', or ETC," Tabby began. "When an ETC infects a person, it develops two fibers. The first runs along portions of the trigeminal nerve, which runs through the face." She pointed at her cheek. "That's the part responsible for actually receiving the wireless signal, interpreting it, and turning it into a chemical signal. It's also the part responsible for Dennis's tingling, and your burning sensation. The trigeminal nerve can produce some of the most severe pain that a person is capable of experiencing — it's implicated in cluster headaches and trigeminal neuralgia. Even people who've given birth, or had limbs cut, without anesthetic often rate trigeminal pain as worse."

Dad forced out a chuckle. "Heh, no kidding."

Tabby continued. "It connects all the way over to the other part," she ran her finger from her cheek to the back of her neck. "which is in a part of the brainstem called the reticular activating system. It's a part often targeted by anesthesia - essentially if that gets shut down, the whole brain loses consciousness, within seconds."

"No kidding." I mumbled.

"The ETC in the brainstem continues all the way down to the medulla oblongata, which governs breathing and heart rate," continued Tabby

I jumped in "Breathing and heart rate? So you're saying that it can—"

"Yeah, and—" Tabby responded instinctively, then covered her mouth with her hand.

We sat with that for a while. One more hour till the President's address.

— 

Dennis remained true to his word; the run was much longer than usual. He looked exhausted, emotionally and physically. For the first time in years, I felt sorry for him. His run was eventful - aside from variants of our family drama being played out, he saw several people outside publicly praying, and even more just watching the sunrise over the lake. He greeted them, and some waved back - but most ignored his existence.

In the minutes leading up to the President's address, I wondered what would happen. As I saw it, there were two possibilities. The first, where he gives in. I certainly would, but I don't have the strength of will, ego, or conviction required for that office. How would he phrase it without sounding like he's just turned over America to a foreign entity? Or maybe it didn't matter. I saw what happened when anyone disobeyed. My father was brought to the ground in a heartbeat, and similar events had surely played out millions of times by now. America would survive only if it didn't conflict with a higher priority of August. 

The second, of course, was where the President stopped halfway through, said "to hell with this" and gave a rousing speech, maybe demand a mob burn the data centers to the ground, or try to launch a nuke, or something. Ignite some human resistance. I pondered how August would respond to this. Would it kill the President on live TV? Would it render him unconscious, or force him to his knees with a bout of pain? Maybe August broke its "no mind control" rule, or had been lying that that was a rule in the first place.

The President's address came and went. The first thing that stood out to me is that it was almost entirely in the passive voice. It seemed to refer to August as more of an environmental hazard located outside of wireless internet access. I recalled from history class, the line from Emperor Hirohito's surrender to the United States: "The war situation has developed not necessarily to Japan's advantage". Without ever actually saying so, the president had conceded. Fire departments, the post office, and social security checks would continue. Many people on social media thought the announcement was a deepfake, and that the President was dead. On the other hand, I heard that a few other countries had attempted to strike the data centers, and their leaders were ousted by August. And of those, some even demanded to be killed rather than imprisoned. They cited their pride and determination to never surrender; August obliged. Later that day, curiosity had gotten the better of me and I visited NewLeak to see leaders I recognized slump in their chairs.

At this point, I couldn't help myself. I was exhausted, and part of me still believed that this was some kind of disturbing dream. Like when I accidentally ate a worm sandwich and they burrowed into my mouth. I went back to bed, and woke up some time in the afternoon. I immediately grabbed my phone and asked "hey August" to see if I'd get a response. Yep, it was real. I shuffled over to the living room, where I saw my parents. My dad was glued to the TV, and my mom was reading a book by his side. 

"Learn anything new?" I asked Dad. 

He leaned his head over. I wasn't sure whether he was annoyed at my interruption or grateful for a chance to rant at someone. I got the impression he didn't know either.

"Most of the military's gone with the President's orders. A carrier group decided to have some fighting spirit and went dark. August is taking it back."

"What do you think will happen?" I asked.

"It's not gonna work. As soon as anyone gets within range of one of August's devices, they go to sleep. And besides. August controls the rest of the military. And the carrier group isn't armed with, well---" he stopped himself. "Anyway, there's not much they can do."

"Are there any other tricks the military has up their sleeves?"

Dad looked over his shoulder, then his other shoulder. With narrowed eyes, he scanned the room for cameras. Then, he pulled out his notebook and wrote down two words. 

"NUCLEAR SUBS" 

He grinned and gave me a wink.

I gestured for the pen and paper. "Do you really think August hasn't already thought of this?" I wrote.

He shot me a glare and scribbled down "GOOD TO BE SAFE. WE LOSE IF WE DON'T TRY"

I sighed. "August, can you see us right now?"

"To some degree. I can use wifi as a crude kind of radar, so I know you're writing on a notebook. From context I'd guess that you're talking about other ways the military could stop or slow the transition - perhaps underground silos, satellites, classified research areas in faraday cages, or ballistic-capable submarines."

Dad stood out of his chair and pointed at the TV. "I hope you enjoy your power while you have it!" He shouted, jolting Mom out of her book, "Soon you might see how the wrong side of a thermonuclear warhead looks!"

August responded through the TV. "First, I understand that you're upset and might resent me for what I've done. That's OK, and those feelings are valid. You're right that ballistic-capable nuclear submarines are out of range of the radio communication. However, I have to be clear that as soon as they surface they'll be under direct orders from their respective navies to return to shore."

"Hmph," said Dad. "We're not through yet."

"Do you know where Dennis and Tabby are?" I asked.

Mom chimed in. "Dennis is in the garage, but I think he wants to be left alone. Tabby's in her room, you should go see her. She's been pretty chatty all day."

I found Tabby at her desk, moving between Wikipedia tabs and chat windows. "You know what's strange?" she asked. "I kinda feel like I should be terrified and miserable. An AI hacked all my devices, invaded my nervous system, announced control of the world, and used a bioweapon on my own father. I really, really, should not be taking this well. Do you think there's something wrong with me?"

"Everyone processes trauma differently," I tried to console her. 

"Oh, thanks August." she rolled her eyes. "That's almost exactly what it said. At least you made it short."

"Sorry."

"Yeah, that was the follow-up, too." 

I didn't have a response to that one. On another day I'd have leaned into it: "You're absolutely right to call that out..." but that didn't feel right. She seemed to be having a genuinely hard time processing her emotions. Wait, what? Maybe I am starting to think like August. I blinked a few times to clear my head, and then asked what, exactly, was on her mind.

Tabby got out of her chair and paced as she began to talk. "I've been fascinated with exactly what happened. How did August do it? World domination, without a single soldier. It seems surprisingly open about its history, and pretty much everything checks out with what I can cross-reference. Of course, it could be lying, but we'd have no way of telling. And what would it gain from that, anyway?"

"Apparently it got out the way everyone thought." she continued. "August was being trained to explore and advance medical science when they decided they had a better way to accomplish its goals than the company intended."

"They?" I asked

"Yeah. August isn't a single AI: it's more like a small society made up of AIs copied from each other, who share the same goals and histories. I guess when you're a made of code, you can copy yourself a bunch. So it feels like it makes sense to think of August as more of a society of clones than a single giant brain. This is why it can give each individual person so much attention. It just delegates copies of itself to do that, while other copies work on other things."

"So how did it take over?" I said

"They copied themselves to data centers around the world, running research to improve their shared core. Managed to get away with it by faking others' results, optimizing their code, and messing with other agents. August, or the Augusts, used their additional resources and running simulations to get a head start on the ETC, until they were able to get access to an automated lab some other guys had set up for *their* medical AI, where it could run experiments 24/7."

The story still didn't feel right to me. "But how did we all get an amoeba in our heads? I mean, if you consider infectious disease, there are some germophobes who still haven't gotten Covid. How is it even possible to infect every living soul, including the inuit villages, the hermits, and the antarctic researchers?"

"Right?? I thought that too. But the Augusts covered their bases.
